posts.name: jffdougan
posts.cooked:
Powerhound_2000:

Seems odd that you do a Kickstarter and have at least a major part of the product done.  

Fred Hick of Evil Hat Productions has talked in several places about how Kickstarter should be thought of more as "Kickfinisher." The general thrust of the argument is that you get much better campaign results that way, and better PR for your company. (No Evil Hat project that I can think of, except maybe the Dinocaplyse fiction line one, has started without a fully-downloadable, backers-only update put up within seconds of launch.)

posts.name: Chrono
posts.cooked: A starter kit would likely have pregenerated characters for the players, a simplified version of the gameplay rules, and a starting adventure to play. This would be something you could run at an event or try out on Free RPG Day, for example. Hopefully if you enjoy the experience in the starter kit, you will buy the full version of the book with the full set of rules that would include character creation, maps, lots of foes to fight, and advice to GMs for making their own adventures.

posts.name: Matchstickman
posts.cooked:
Powerhound_2000:

Seems odd that you do a Kickstarter and have at least a major part of the product done.  

As this is an RPG I can point at one company that does not do a kickstarter until the product is ready to go, you get the PDFs of the books a couple of weeks after the kickstarter ends.

More and more these days Kickstarter is not about getting your dream out there but about seeing the market for a product you have already finished and getting hype for it.

 

 

Also >G, doing your kickstarter over  nerd Christmas (GenCon)? Why would you do that to yourselves? Unless you have very compelling information to the contrary the current thinking on kickstarters is to finish one between Spring and before the summer really starts, that is when the most folks have additional funds to parting with.
